Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

vignette:
Jorge is a 26-year-old man who came to the United States from El Salvador four years ago, after surviving a period of torture at the hands of local gang members who suspected him of informing to the police. For three days, he was held in a concrete room, beaten, and threatened with death while his captors questioned him. The worst moment came when they brought in a man he recognized from his neighborhood, forced him to watch as they hurt the man, and then told Jorge that the same would happen to everyone he loved if he ever spoke to authorities again. After his release, Jorge fled north, leaving behind his wife and young daughter; the divorce came two years later, when the distance and his silence became too much for the marriage to bear.

Now Jorge works as a maid in a chain hotel, cleaning rooms on a floor where he rarely has to interact with guests. The work is solitary, and that suits him. But certain things have become nearly impossible to manage. When he sees a dark sedan in the parking lot that resembles the car his captors used, his chest tightens and he feels a surge of panic that forces him to retreat into the stairwell until the car is gone. He has also stopped watching television entirely after a news segment about gang violence in Central America sent him into a shaking, tearful state that lasted hours. Even positive emotions have become dangerous: a few months ago, a guest smiled warmly at him in the hallway and thanked him for his work, and Jorge felt a confusing wave of dread that he could not explain, only that the warmth felt like a trap, like kindness that might precede betrayal. That evening, he smoked three cigarettes in a row on the fire escape, trying to calm the sense that something bad was about to happen.

Jorge's sleep is broken. He wakes multiple times during the night, often sitting up in bed and scanning the room for threats before he can orient himself to where he is. If his roommate brushes against him accidentally in the dark, Jorge flinches violently, his heart pounding. He has come to believe that strangers approaching him-even a guest asking for directions or a coworker walking toward him in the break room-carry some hidden threat, and he has begun avoiding eye contact entirely, keeping his head down as a way to stay invisible. These moments of fear, triggered by a car or a face or a sudden touch, feed directly into his vigilance: each time he startles, he becomes more convinced that danger is everywhere, and that he must stay alert or be caught off guard again.

To manage this constant sense of threat, Jorge has developed a set of strategies that he relies on daily. He avoids anyone in uniform-police officers, security guards, even hotel maintenance workers in their blue shirts-because the authority they represent reminds him of the power his captors held over him. He will change his route through the hotel to avoid passing the front desk if a security guard is standing there. If a coworker brings up anything related to violence or crime, Jorge quickly changes the subject or walks away, because being reminded of the event by others feels like being dragged back into that room. The smoking has become a near-constant habit, a way to create a small pocket of control when the world feels unsafe. But these strategies have a cost: the more he avoids, the more he interprets his own behavior as proof that the world is dangerous. Each time he retreats from a car or a uniform, the relief is temporary, and the fear settles deeper. He has started to notice that his avoidance actually makes triggers appear more frequently-now every sedan in the lot catches his eye, every uniformed figure seems to be walking toward him, and even a guest's friendly smile feels like a warning sign he must decode.

The cycle has tightened over the past year. Jorge's manager has commented on his jumpiness, and his roommate has asked why he smokes so much. Jorge has no answer that makes sense to them. What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning two weeks ago when a guest-a middle-aged man in a dark suit-approached him in the hallway and asked for extra towels. Jorge froze, dropped his cart, and ran to the supply closet, where he stayed for twenty minutes, shaking and unable to breathe. After that, he could not go back to work. He is afraid that he is losing his mind, and he is even more afraid that if he does not find a way to stop the fear, he will lose the only job he has, and then there will be nothing left.
